## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. That could be a learning problem or a budget problem, and nothing so far tells them apart. Its design looks reasonable: per-cell features, a pooling head over each brick's footprint, and a pooled DONE/value head. Its weak points are a receptive field of only 5×5 before the head, no global context in the per-cell features, and a short budget of 131k steps with 4 PPO epochs. gamma=0.95 also discounts the +1 exact-build bonus a lot over episodes of 10–33 steps. Following the suggested round-1 split, the three candidates are: (a) a recipe-only change (2 epochs for about 1.86× the samples, gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95); (b) an architecture change at about the same FLOPs (residual 3×3 trunk with a 7×7 receptive field and pooled global context fed into each cell), using the default recipe; (c) both together. Because dev success may stay at 0, I will rank by training success and training signals.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials scored 0 on both dev and training success. None failed, and all finished in 60–80 s against a 900 s limit, so the FLOP budget limits training, not time. Two epochs with gamma 0.99 (about 230k steps) did not help, and neither did a deeper residual trunk with global context. So the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. Both networks flatten all height layers into channels at the first 1×1 layer. To judge a brick, the network must then work out the landing layer, check that the target is missing at that layer on every footprint cell, and check that nothing below gets sealed. That is hard to learn from this layout. I now test (1) a stronger push for more samples, with 1 PPO epoch and about 426k steps, and (2) a layer-wise network. It applies shared 2D convolutions to every height layer, with the layers below and above as inputs, scores footprints within each layer, and then combines the layers with a logsumexp.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success, for both seeds. The changes so far did not help: more samples (up to 405k with 1 PPO epoch), gamma 0.99, a residual trunk with global context, and a per-layer weight-shared network. Since training success is also 0, the bottleneck is learning itself, not generalisation. Wall time was only 60–220 s, so time is not the constraint; the FLOP budget is. One lever we have not tested is how fast PPO can sharpen the policy. With about 250 actions, a near-uniform start, clip 0.2, ent_coef 0.01 and only about 30–100 updates, the sampled policy may never become peaked enough to finish exact builds. These proposals use much smaller batches per update (more updates), lower entropy, and a higher lr or wider clip. They also test attention-based global context under the same aggressive recipe. Because no training signal other than success was reported, the diagnosis is uncertain. The world may also differ from its description.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success, for both seeds. The changes tried were recipe-only (1–2 epochs, gamma 0.97–0.99, faster sharpening, more updates), trunk changes (residual layers, global context, attention) and a layer-wise net that combined layers with logsumexp. None moved training success above 0, so the bottleneck is learning itself, not generalisation. More samples alone did not help: even about 400k steps got nothing. The likely missing piece is the head. The current pooling head squeezes features to 32 channels and then takes the max, min and mean over the footprint. That is a weak way to work out exactly where a brick lands and whether every cell it fills matches the target at that height. The final round tests heads that see the whole footprint (raw observation plus trunk features) through a learned convolution shaped like the footprint. It also tests a layer-wise net that chooses the landing layer with a learned softmax gate. Every run uses 1 PPO epoch to get the most samples.
